entry.title: I Built a Road Safety Snakes & Ladders Game in Class 11… and Then Let It Rot for 2 Years 💀🐍🎲
entry.summary:
Hey devs, Ishant here 👋 This one’s ancient. Back in Class 11, my teacher told me: So I built a Snakes & Ladders — Road Safety Edition in Python. Then the teacher never checked it. And the project just… sat on my PC for 2.0 years like a forgotten save file. 💀 Until today. It’s classic Snakes & Ladders, but education-flavored: 🚦 Follow traffic rules → ladder Instead of “oops bad luck”, the game straight-up tells you: Overspeeding? Get cooked. Red light jump? Down you go. Follow rules? Free ladder, king 👑 Here’s the fun constraint: ❌ I was NOT allowed to design my own board. I had to use a specific road safety image. Which meant: Measuring tile size in pixels
Calculating player movement manually Dividing & multiplying coordinates for every tile Aligning sprites so they don’t drift into another universe Ironically, if I was allowed to design my own board, this would’ve taken hours. Instead, it took pain. Dice-based movement Snakes & ladders with random road safety messages
Sound effects: Dice roll Snake (aka accident 💀) Ladder (bonus 😎) Start menu + About Developer screen
Keyboard shortcuts: Space → Roll dice Esc → Exit Packaged into a Windows EXE (no Python needed)
Built in about two weeks with Class 11 energy and zero fear. Python Pygame Packaged for Windows Open-sourced under MIT because why not This is NOT: A commercial game A viral hit A masterpiece It’s just an old project that deserved to see daylight instead of rotting forever. GitHub (code + releases): https://github.com/0pen-Sourcer/Snakes-and-ladders-Road-Safety-Edition/ Anyway, that’s it. No “lessons learned”. — Ishant 🖤

entry.title: Part 7 — What GenAI Engineering Actually Is
entry.summary: GenAI engineering is often misunderstood. It’s not prompt writing. It’s systems engineering under uncertainty. Experienced software engineers already know: How to design interfaces How to manage failure How to reason about tradeoffs How to operate systems at scale These skills transfer cleanly. What changes is the component behavior. Models: Are probabilistic Have opaque internals Change underneath you Require containment Engineering discipline matters more, not less. A GenAI engineer: Designs constraints Owns system behavior Treats models as replaceable components Optimizes for reliability over novelty This is not a new profession. It’s a specialization. GenAI doesn’t replace software engineering. It exposes whether it was there in the first place.
